utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Our proceedings are delayed because of the fact that the recording system was not ready for 1415 hours. We will start. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honours. I do apologise before we start, I will be very brief, speaking on behalf of all of my colleagues from the Defence teams, in fact the issue is related to the Rule 71, the positions that we have to perform next week. We were informed by our case manager, our colleague, was present and also colleague, Mr. Lazarevic, that certain instructions with regard to the possibility for the other Defence teams related to the examination or cross-examination of the witness of the other Defence team will not be permitted and I respectfully ask for the ratification of that issue because our opinion is that on the basis of Rule 21 of Article 21 of the Statute where the exact and very precise formulations with regard to the rights of the accused, namely with the possibility to pose the questions to examine the witnesses of -- from one proceedings will be to some extent valid, so we think that the other Defence teams should be able to pose certain number of questions with regard to the -- to their case immediately after the examination-in-chief of one or first Defence team in question. My opinion, my personal opinion regarding to the possible prospects of the case, I'm speaking on behalf of my client, Mr. Blagoje Simic, that I don't think that it will be so many possibilities or that we shall significantly affect the frame of time that was imposed to us so it's rather a matter of principle that we think that should be respected. And also I think my colleague Mr. Lukic has something to add. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to join with what my learned friend, Mr. Pantelic, has said. I think that one thing that could present a problem for me is that I really think that as you have made it possible throughout the proceedings for the other Defences can question certain witnesses regarding those relevant things that relate to their clients. I think that depositions are also evidence and also it can be within Article 85. So I think we can completely adhere to your instructions regarding the time limits, but then we should also be allowed, within that limit, if any other Defence does wish to pose any questions to the witness, that this should be possible during the examination-in-chief. On the other hand, in that situation, we could provide summaries to the Prosecution if we did have topics that we wanted to question the witness about so that the Prosecution would not feel compromised otherwise. This way we're in the situation which through cross-examination a new topic could be introduced and it's possible, I think that perhaps I have maybe a topic that I would like to question a witness from another Defence. This could of course be done within the time limit given in agreement with my colleagues. Otherwise, I would have to be in the situation of asking my colleague to ask questions that he was not really very familiar with. So we could use the time that you have determined for the depositions but would also respect our full right to question the witnesses and thereby properly represent our clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What I need clarification on --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position, I don't know if my colleagues will support me, is that we do not wish to exceed the limit given for the examination-in-chief. If a team for a witness is given 40 minutes and if my colleague finishes in 30 minutes and I do have questions, then I would like to be -- for it to be possible for me to ask my questions within those remaining ten minutes of course the Prosecution would be informed of that in advance. This is a joint case and there are certain things that cross over from witness to witness. We are talking about depositions but we will not lose anything as far as the schedule of the depositions is concerned and which we have agreed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just want to be clear about what you have said. You are saying that within the time limited for examination-in-chief, if the calling counsel does not exhaust 40 minutes, then any other counsel should exhaust the rest of the time, within the 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, but this is not to be a rule but just an exception if there are questions for a particular witness, it would not apply to each witness. If a colleague did not exhaust his full allotted time, and if another counsel wishes to ask questions, then they should be allowed to use that remaining time to put their questions just like we did in the proceedings here. But I would just like to remark this would be an exception and as I noted, perhaps this would only be the case with one witness out of the total number of witnesses. At a meeting with the registrar, we were informed that the registry cannot give us any decisions regarding this so this is why we are addressing the Trial Chamber so that we know what our position is in the course of the depositions. So if, within the allotted time for the examination-in-chief, if there is some time left over, that it be possible for another counsel to ask questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution briefly be heard on this Your Honour taking you to the relevant section of the relevant Article and the relevant Rule. Mr. Pantelic quoted Article 21(D) of the Statute. The correct Article is Article 21(E), which guarantees an accused person the right to examine - I am quoting from it - or have examined the witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance of examination of witnesses on his behalf. The witnesses called by the three accused in -- for the depositions, the purposes of taking depositions are not witnesses against him, against any of the other accused, so the article -- so the Statute doesn't enshrine a right to cross-examine witnesses who are called by parties who are presenting basically a joint Defence. If you then move directly to Rule 71 under which depositions authorised and that's the only authority for -- under which the Court may order depositions, Rule 71(C) says, I'll just read it: "If the motion is granted, the party at whose request the deposition is to be taken shall give reasonable notice to the other party who shall have the right to attend the taking of the deposition and cross-examine the person whose deposition is being taken." The rule, in my submission, is clearly capable of only one interpretation, that is the party calling it, either each of the three accused calls the party and the other party which here, is the Prosecution, it's not the other accused, has the right to cross-examine. No right is given under either the rules or the Statute for co-accused to cross-examine a witness called by one of them who is not against them. If the witness was against one of the other accused, of course they would have a right to cross-examine if it was what you call a cut throat Defence between the through defendants or three accused, that's not the case here. So my submission is brief, the Rules and the Article just don't provide for it and only the Prosecution may cross-examine in a deposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour, just a brief issue. This is a joinder case so practically and theoretically we've seen that on many occasions that even the witness from the other Defence team might be considered as so-called hostile witness to the other Defence team. So in joinder case, it -- there are some differences with regard to the single accused and the single number of witnesses from one or the other side. So we witness it on many occasions here that if the witness of the -- for the one Defence team raised certain issue it should be clarified because it's interferes, there is certain impact to the Defence of the other Defence team. So I think it's clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will take time and will give its ruling in due course. We'll start with the witness. Can the witness make the solemn declaration, please, while standing up. Can the witness stand up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, please sit down. Mr. Lukic or Mr. Krgovic, it's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, since you had some health problems when you came to The Hague in order to testify, I just would like to tell you that if you feel -- if you don't feel well or feel any difficulties in the course of this examination, please let us know and we will make a break in the proceedings. We will try not to disturb you too much so that we would not put any strain on your health. I would like you to answer briefly so that we would cover all the topics that you were called here to testify about as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell me your name?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Svetozar Vasovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 8th of August, 1936 in the village of Trepca near Andrijevica, the republic Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell us what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I am a Montenegrin by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, are you married?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm married.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of your wife?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: My wife is from Slavonski Brod, she's a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, what school did you complete?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I completed the high school and after that, I finished the teacher's college and my whole life I have been working as a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell me, did you serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What year was that and where?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I served in 1961 and 1962 in the town of Stip in the republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After leaving the army, did you receive any rank?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I was -- I was a corporal and then a squad leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell us since when have you been living in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I have been living in Bosanski Samac from August 1958 and actually I started to work in 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where you worked?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I worked in the whole of the Samac municipality. First, I worked in the village of Kruskovo Polje then I was transferred to the village of Obudovac. From Obudovac I came back to Hrvatska Tisina, from Hrvatska Tisina I went to work in Gornja Slatina, from Gornja Slatina, I came back to Hrvatska Tisina again and after that to Samac where I actually worked until the end of my career.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you came back from the army, did you have a war assignment in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did just like everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me where was your war assignment?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any particular task or were you just a member of the reserves?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I was just a member of the reserves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell us if you had a nickname?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any nicknames, not as a child, nobody amongst the pupils gave me a nickname or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a nickname Obrva?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No, this is the first time that I'm hearing of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mrs. Hajra Drljacic?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, just by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did she ever call you by that nickname, did she ever address you?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think that we ever actually talked to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell us, before the outbreak of the war in Bosanski Samac, were you a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: The league of communists of Yugoslavia and after that, of the SDP and then after that the socialist party of Republika Srpska, of which I am a member still today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me when you met -- became a member of the socialist party of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: In February 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the socialist party of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the political life?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, and where did you live in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I lived and I am still living in the street of Djuro Djakovic 29 and now Jovana Cvijica 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, I would like to ask you briefly, very briefly in a couple of sentences to describe for us the situation in Bosanski Samac immediately in the few months immediately prior to the 16th and 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, the situation was very difficult because in the neighbouring republic of Croatia, war was being waged so this seriously affected the situation in Bosanski Samac as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were the relationships between the people of different ethnicity disrupted?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were beginning to separate or there were divisions along ethnic lines, they were just beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And how did this manifest itself?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: In a pretty ugly manner, I have to say, because until then, the heterogeneous composition of Samac lived as one and then suddenly this division came about and that really had an affect on many things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell us whether you noticed if your co-citizens were beginning to arm themselves, did you notice any patrols which could maybe begin to worry you or other Samac citizens?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, everybody in Samac could notice something like that, all the citizens were arming themselves. There were patrols in town, everybody had their own patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice whether your co-citizens of Muslim ethnicity were arming themselves, did they have patrols?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were -- you could see them around the mosque and then also in the surrounding streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you pass through the surrounding villages with the Croat population?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did once or twice as I was returning from the village of Donja Slatina towards Samac. At a place called Grebnice where there is this intersection, one road goes to Orasje and the other goes to Samac and a patrol stopped me, they were wearing camouflage uniforms, they asked for ID. I noticed then one of my pupils and two others who were there together and when they noticed me, they said, "Oh, this is all right. He can go ahead." So that's how I managed to pass through unimpeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to the evidence on the basis that it's outside, well outside the matters provided in the summary which, as I can see, is limited to the witness' duties at crossing exchanges in the events before -- during the takeover the Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just meant this by way of a brief introduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber had given instructions yesterday in view of the health of the witness. The other point is that so many witnesses have discussed this, the rising tensions, the arming of along ethnic lines, there is no dispute about it anymore. Please go directly to the Red Cross, the exchanges as given in the summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, I'm just going to ask you whether you know Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How long?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: From the 1970s, I think, perhaps a bit later well somewhere around there, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you frequent the cafe of Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you acquaintances or friends, I'm just interested in the kind of relationship you had?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, acquaintances, but I was friends with everybody and there is no need for me to say anything different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, I'm not going to ask you anything about the events that preceded the 16th and 17th of April or about the episodes that followed. My examination is now going to focus on your engagement in the Red Cross. Can you tell us whether, before the war, you were included in the work of the Red Cross organisation in the territory of the municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: You know what, every teacher is involved in Red Cross work. We have Red Cross courses at schools, we teach classes in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you president of some organisation?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I was even president of the municipal committee of the Red Cross of the municipality of Samac and I insisted on a great many things for the sake of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just before the war broke out, what position did you hold in the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, during those days, the 18th or the 19th of April, did you get any kind of call or summons to join the work of the Red Cross, can you describe this for me?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Right after the outbreak or rather the shooting between the 16th and 17th, one knows what the situation was like then, doesn't one? And then I was called from the local commune because people knew that I was an activist of the Red Cross anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, can I just ask you to speak a bit slower?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I was called from the local commune because they knew that I had always been an activist, that I was a teacher, and that my ethics corresponds to that of the Red Cross so they called me on the 18th and then I came to the local commune as you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you go to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What was it that you agreed upon at that meeting, did you give people different assignments or what did you do?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: The Red Cross did exist but we established a proper one, Milorad Mihajlovic, who was president of the municipal Red Cross in view of everything that was going on made us aware of all the activities that the Red Cross should be engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You'll have to clarify this for us. So the Red Cross did exist?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And your meeting was devoted to giving various assignments to people so it wasn't that you were setting up an organisation from scratch?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, it was just giving various assignments to people, continuing the work of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have a document shown to the witness now please it is internally marked PDB 3/3. Your Honours, this is going to be the only document that we are going to introduce during the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, would you tell me whether you saw this document before?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document that was issued to me after the municipal organisation of the Red Cross continued to work. A few days later, I don't know exactly when, I got this decision explaining that in this emergency situation, I was still a member of the Red Cross and that I was supposed to continue working. To tell you the truth, I have a copy of this document here too, see, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There is no need for that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the Prosecution doesn't object, I would like this document to receive a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's no objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D141/3 and ter for the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, during those first days, that is to say, after the appointment of yours, what was the specific assignment that you were given?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: We met every morning at the Red Cross office. We were given assignments. We were told who was supposed to do what. I got a delivery vehicle and they said that I was supposed to go to various local communes to talk to the commissioners there so that they would collect milk, food, and all other indispensable supplies so that they would be brought into the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you contact with when you say "commissioners," are you talking about Red Cross commissioners?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Red Cross commissioners, only Red Cross. It's only with the Red Cross that we worked. I mean we from the municipal organisation because we had local organisations of the Red Cross there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were they organised according to local communes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: They were, but in this case, it was the president who was in charge of a great many things but they had reached agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Vasovic, when, from the representatives of the Red Cross of these local communes, when you got food from them, where did you take that food and what was done with it then?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: You know what, the municipal organisation of the Red Cross in Samac established certain points, there were a few of them. I remember the local commune, at the local market, in Donja Mahala, there were commissioners there as well who were in charge of the following: When food would be brought in, then it would be distributed to the needy population, I mean it was milk most of the time, and eggs, and I was the one who brought that food in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: During those first days after the 16th and 17th of April, was food distributed without any lists or according to certain lists or how was this dealt with during these first days?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: There was no market, there was no milk and it was distributed to everyone, the entire population, especially to the neediest ones because we knew more or less who the needy ones were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, were some lists made for the distribution of this aid according to various parts of town?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in the following way: The centre for social welfare had its own lists and in the previous period, they assisted the needy population. Those lists were brought to the Red Cross in order to supplement them, in order to see who should be the recipients of this aid. Again, there was no difference involved whatsoever. The entire population was entitled to receive whatever could be obtained from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The list you mentioned, was this the list of beneficiaries of social welfare?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the list. That's the list from the social welfare centre but we also made a list, and our own list had certain additions in relation to the social welfare centre's list so we as a Red Cross used our own list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, when these lists were compiled, did you distinguish between the members of various ethnic groups or did you hand it out to everyone equally?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, to everyone equally. At these various points, I know personally, because I went to each and every one of them, it is for the most part Muslims who were distributing this aid, everything that was handed out, it was Muslims who were handing it go out in Donja Mahala for example, Dzigera Pistoljevic for instance, he was in charge of all of Donja Mahala, also here at the market, again, there was a Muslim. His nickname is Mrgud. He is deceased but I have to say that he is the one who distributed this aid with the assistance of others. So they were there wherever this aid was being distributed and there were no distinctions made along ethnic lines whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, in addition to yourself, who was employed at the Red Cross out of the employees there?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: There was the president, Milorad Mihajlovic, then Velimir Maslic, Anka Jovanovic, she is a social worker anyway, and Milka Petkovic. There were people who helped out every now and then, but these were the people who bore the brunt of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, tell me, where were the offices of the Red Cross where you worked?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: The Red Cross offices were at the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This building where the local commune is, does it have a name of some kind, what do people call it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: It's the pensioner's building. It's the pensioner's building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Vasovic, where were your offices approximately?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Upstairs, upstairs, that's where we had an office although we used another one too but that's where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown a photograph, D36/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, please take a look at that. Could you take that pointer that's there right next to you?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us on that photograph whether you can see the windows?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No, you can can't see them, they're on the back side on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Where is the entrance roughly into the Red Cross premises?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: It's on the other side, the entrance in order to go upstairs, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, to go upstairs. Tell me, Mr. Vasovic, in addition to yourself or rather in addition to the Red Cross, were there any other offices there at the pensioner's building?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: There was the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about the social welfare centre?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: They were there too but they worked together with us and that's why I'm saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Vasovic, in this building, is that where the Secretariat for National Defence had its offices, that dealt with work obligation?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Where were these offices?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: They were on the ground floor, there are two entrances here actually. The front entrance where these two vehicles are, and behind this blue vehicle, there is an entrance too, I mean I think that there are three rooms there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm only interested in this entrance here to the pensioner's building?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Vasovic, these offices that dealt with work obligation, the ones on the ground floor that you mentioned and the offices of the Red Cross and the civilian -- are you trying to say -- is there any physical link between the two?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: None whatsoever except the ceiling.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness now be shown document D85/3 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, in terms of the transcript, page 19, we've got a question which isn't finished and then we've got two answers following but the first answer on line 5 is in the form of a question, could you confirm whether the witness was asking himself a question and answering it too?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my question was these offices for the work obligation that were in the -- on the ground floor in which you mentioned and these offices of the Red Cross and the civilian defence, were they physically connected? Mr. Vasovic, this is because the transcript, we would just like to repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not physically connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell me, these people that you mentioned who distributed milk and worked as part of the Red Cross, these trustees, these commissioners?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: They were practically registered as Red Cross activists?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were members of the Red Cross and that is precisely why they were engaged in the work and even without that, we were looking for people who wanted to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this document. Do you recognise these people?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did they work together with you at the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Together, all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell me, what was the ethnicity of these people?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Everyone is there, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs and by names, also if it's necessary, I will tell you who is who. I know these people, they are my friends from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that will be necessary. Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell me in the Red Cross and in those offices upstairs that you used together with the members of the civilian protection and the centre for social work, did you have a telephone there?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was one single telephone but we, as the Red Cross, didn't have our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did all of those services use that one telephone?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the services, the Red Cross, the centre for social work that was with us and also these down there for the work obligation. If somebody called us on the telephone, we could always have this conversation with them and that's how it was for everybody. Everybody could use the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me did people who were working downstairs in the work obligation also receive telephone calls through that telephone?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Some of us always went to get them or a messenger went either to convey the message to them or for them to actually come to the phone so that they could get the information themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who most frequently answered the phone of the employees who were in those offices?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I think that he was constantly on the phone, Ljubo Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And while we are still on the telephone topic, Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell me, what was the situation with telephones in general in that period in early May in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No, the telephones were not working, they were all switched off. I think that in the town of Samac, only perhaps three or four telephones were operating, where and how, I don't know, but only three or four of them worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally have a telephone in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I still have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And was it working in that period?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell us when the telephones started to work again in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I don't know. I simply cannot remember when they started to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is what year, 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: It would more be 1993 rather than 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell me, did you have to submit another request for a telephone or did they have to again --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Although I had my own number, and -- in spite of that, I still had to go to the post office again and submit a request not only myself, but all the people who had telephones had to resubmit their requests although many of them were not there so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't need a really detailed explanation but I just wanted to touch upon this since you mentioned the telephones. Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell me, did you hear in those initial days after the war broke out in Bosanski Samac, that some of your fellow citizens were arrested?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear where they were holding them, where those people were?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber what you heard, where were these people detained?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: They were detained in the police station and also on the premises of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, did you ever have the opportunity to go to these premises that you just talked about?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when was the first time, approximately, you don't have to give us the exact date, that you went to those premises and how did it come about that you went there?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I think I went there in the month of May. I went there to visit the place because I heard that there was some people that I knew very well there, and as a representative of the Red Cross, I wanted to see the conditions, the way they really were. I was sent by the president of the Red Cross, Milorad Mihajlovic and Velimir Maslic to do that. I went there, I looked around, and I saw what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell us what you saw, how did those people look?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, they looked very bad. They were exhausted, underfed, bad in all aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any people among them who were beaten with visible signs of beating?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were, of course, of course. To my astonishment, I saw that and I was, simply put, surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know those people?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, almost all of them. I can't tell you each one by name, but more or less I know every one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell me, did you inform anybody of your superiors of how those people looked in the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Everything that I did, any place that I visited, anywhere that I was sent on be -- by the president of the Red Cross, Velimir Maslic or anyone else, I would always report back about everything that I had seen and everything about the situation and then they would be the ones who would take the appropriate steps and do what was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you went on that occasion, as far as I understood, you went to the premises of the SUP for the first time?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the security station or SUP. That is the security station, but the SUP was actually in the department store.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, did you have any instructions during your visits to ask those people or to inform them if they wanted to go to an exchange or that they were being sought for an exchange, did you have the authority to talk about that with them?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I never went of my own free will, I went there by duty and that was one of my tasks when I go and of course when I was instructed to do so, I would ask who wanted to be exchanged. I would note all of that down. After noting it down, I would go back to the Red Cross and I would give this list to -- and I would hand in this list that I had compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, on that occasion when you spoke to those people, on that day, did you also visit the TO or did you go to the TO on another occasion?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the TO on another occasion, the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the people that you talked with and the persons that you asked if they wanted to go on an exchange or not?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: In the SUP, yes, of course. Franjo from Prude, Franjo Barukcic was there, and also the person who was the chief of the SUP was there, what was his name? I can't remember his name right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of SUP?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: He was before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well if you can't remember it doesn't matter?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: And Hasan Jasarevic was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what did those people tell you that -- did they want to go?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they said that they wanted to go to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, when was the first time that you went to the premises of the TO?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: After this visit. Again, I was tasked by the president of the Red Cross to ask who wanted to go to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, what did the people who were detained at the Territorial Defence look like?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I got there, it didn't look very good to me. I went inside with Mrs. Milka Markovic -- Petrovic and since the police knew that I was working in the Red Cross because I was wearing the insignia of the Red Cross, so they called everybody out and all of them came out and they were standing in two lines and I was not breathing easily at that time myself and then I asked gentlemen, friends, this is the way I addressed them in the only way that I knew how, because I wasn't feeling comfortable myself, I asked those who want to go for an exchange can apply for that and my colleague, Milka, will write that down and we will convey that to the Red Cross over there and then that will be taken into procedure and then we will see. And they applied and we noted that down. And what you asked me about what they looked like, I wouldn't like to see anybody in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, did you inform your superiors about that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, always. Everything that I saw, I reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell me whether Mrs. Petkovic went with you to visit all those facilities?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, after that first meeting with the people in the Territorial Defence, Milka indicated to me and then to the president of the Red Cross that she couldn't work anymore. To be honest, I also wanted to give my notice and say that I didn't want to do that job anymore because I really couldn't go and visit those people who were so beaten, who were black and blue, who were beaten up, but I remained in that post. I simply don't know why, for humanitarian reasons primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, and after those first visits to the premises of the TO, did you continue to go to the TO on any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the next day I had additional questions about whether people wanted to go on an exchange or not and unfortunately, I saw that people were depressed, they were quiet, they were ill at ease and I was surprised. I was wondering why is it that they were keeping quiet. There was an older man there, we called him Ciko, he was a Muslim. I called him because he liked me because I was involved in sports for a long time. He said -- I told him: "Come to me." And they said -- nobody wanted to say a word and I was -- that's what he said, Ciko, "Sveto nobody wants to say a word," and I was thinking, why, when yesterday you asked who wanted to be exchanged after you left the police came and all of those who had applied to go received a beating and that was the reason why I did not get even the answers that I had come to get.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't inform anyone about which people had applied?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No, I only handed that over to the Red Cross, nobody else knew if somebody was eavesdropping, perhaps, whether the police officers perhaps remembered that by computer, let me put it that way. I don't understand, but each single person who applied for the exchange received a beating from the policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, I would now like to ask you whether later in the course of your work you learned about the evacuation of women and children to Serbia, sometime in mid-May, 1992. Do you know whether the Red Cross did anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was compiling the lists there as well. Buses were leaving, and there were lists. They were also leaving in trains because of the state of affairs in early May, it was very dangerous, really dangerous in Samac at the time, Samac was being shelled a lot and that is why people were afraid and this is why they started to leave Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Vasovic, did you send your family away from Samac?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I'm overjoyed to have done that. I took a car, and I took them to Bijeljina. Since I have relatives in Belgrade, they went to Belgrade from Bijeljina and that is how my family was in Belgrade during those hard times. And I stayed back to work and I remained in God's hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, in addition to what you did, did other people do that too, did they take their families out of Bosanski Samac during those first few days after the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Well yes, yes, all three ethnic groups, everybody was leaving, everybody because there was free passage at first and everybody wanted to leave the town of Samac as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please tell me whether after this evacuation or rather just a minute, please, I'm going to put a question to you before that. Did the Red Cross take part in this evacuation?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: The Red Cross was present everywhere, but this was done by the local communes, local communes for the most part but the Red Cross was present everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was evacuated to Serbia then, the members of which ethnic groups, was it members of one ethnic group only or all?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I assert that it was members of all ethnic groups, all ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, tell me, let's go back to this period now. These people you described a short while ago at the SUP and the TO, why were they detained, do you have any direct knowledge as to why they were detained, did anybody tell you something like that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what I heard, I mean I don't know anything personally, I don't have any firsthand knowledge, all of them were either members of units that belonged to their own people or they had weapons. And most probably that is why they were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, tell me now after this evacuation, in the month of May 1992, did people start coming to the Red Cross asking whether they could leave Samac?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Whether they could leave? Oh, indeed. There were queues, especially of the Muslim population and also there were Croats as well. They came saying that they wanted to go, that's what they asked for now why, because there was fear instilled in everybody's bones and of course they were seeking ways and means of saving their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the situation like concerning ethnic Serbs, did they also come to receive information about the ways in which Samac could be left?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, everybody wanted to save their own lives, everybody wanted to leave and everybody asked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What did the ethnic Serbs say, where did they want to go and where did the Muslims and the Croats want to go?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs mostly wanted to go to Serbia and the Muslims and Croats to Croatia, for the most part, although there were Muslims who went to Serbia too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, tell us, when did you first hear of exchanges of detained persons between the Serb side and the Croat and Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I think it was in the month of May, May or June when agreement was reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time, sometime around the end of May 1992 in Zasavica an exchange was organised?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. I was not present at that exchange but the International Red Cross carried out an exchange so they -- so people crossed the Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since you said that you were not present at that exchange, how come you know?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, people know, everybody knew and I worked at the Red Cross so I knew because Milorad Mihajlovic is president of the Red Cross went to that exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Velimir Maslic, did he also attend that exchange?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Velimir Maslic did, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, I'm going to ask you something in very general terms about how people applied for exchanges. Tell me, did people apply there, at the Red Cross, where you were, very briefly, just in a few sentences, what was the procedure involved?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Milka was involved in these matters, Milka Petkovic and Anka Jovanovic was and I was and if possible, Milorad Mihajlovic if he was there too, they came there in front of the premises of the Red Cross. They entered the office one by one. We wrote down their names and their dates of birth and also their wishes as to where they wanted to go, so then the list would be compiled on that basis and there is not a single person who came or rather single citizen who came and who was interested in leaving whose name was not registered. Everybody's name was registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, tell us, once this list is compiled, what would happen to the list then?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: All these lists were seen first and foremost by the president of the Red Cross and then from there, I would take these lists to the public security station or rather the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. When you'd make this list of persons who applied, who did you send it to?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: It was in our office but in the hands of the president of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did this list go any further, was it the subject of negotiations with the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Not only that, we had a list or rather we had requests that had come from the opposite side from the other side who they were looking for, who was supposed to go. And now, it did not only have to do with the possibilities involved it was also our wish to reunite families whose members were here and there so we wanted to reunite these families and that's how these lists were compiled too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Vasovic, what about people who were detained? So when according to the instructions of your president of the Red Cross and your superiors, when you would finish making these lists in those places of detention where these people were, then what would happen with those lists?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Well you know what these lists did not even come to the Red Cross. This list would go to the SUP, especially as far as detentions are concerned, I mean people who were in detention so of course then they would see that list, and then they would discuss it. And they would make a decision, make decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, these lists of civilians and persons who were detained, did you take these lists somewhere?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, to the head of the SUP at that time and unfortunately, I met him twice and I would never like to see him again, never in my life and if you want to I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Vasovic, what's the name of that man?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: His name is Stevan Todorovic, his nickname is Stiv.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, tell us, why did you say what you said a minute ago? What is it that happened when you took those lists there?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: When I brought the lists, he saw the list of Muslims, Croats, probably -- and with the Court's indulgence, begging your pardon, in this world, there is not the right kind of vocabulary to describe all the derogatory terms that he used when addressing me and he almost [Realtime transcript read in error "also"] beat me up and this happened yet another time. I thought that perhaps the first time he got all worked up, but no, it happened the second time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that we need to clarify something in the transcript. Here on page 32, line 6, here it says and he also beat me up and this is not what witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter said almost beat up. The LiveNote is simply different interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes that will be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, why did Stevan Todorovic threaten you, why did he behave to you in this way, did he say why?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Well the only thing that he said is what have you got to do with this and who is it that you are sending for an exchange. It's as if I were doing it myself as if it weren't the Red Cross. So well let me tell you one more thing: Later on, I went out of my way not to see him again and if you want, I can explain that too. How I went out of my way in order not to see him anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever the list was supposed to be taken in, the list for exchanges, I tried to see whether he was in his office at the SUP. When I would hear that he was there, then I would go to Sava Cancarevic, commander of the police who was far more flexible who was a nicer person to talk to who knew all this and who simply wanted to help at least to a degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you just repeat the name of the police commander who was there?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Sava Cancarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just a bit perplexed by this sentence I see in the transcript, I didn't quite understand you either. What is it that Stevan Todorovic said to you, who was in charge of sending people for exchanges, why was he shouting at you?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: He wanted to do everything on his own, everything. How should I put this? He was so self-confident. He thought that he knew everything, that he could do everything and that's why he behaved this way. I beg your pardon for using this expression, but he was really cocky and he bossed around the members of other ethnic groups and see how he behaved to me too, although I'm orthodox by religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, tell me, these lists that you've been talking about, did you take them anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: To the military command, the military command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you hand these lists to?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: A messenger, always waited for me in front of the door I would give the messenger the lists and I would wait in a separate room outside until they would finish that and then when they would finish, then this would be returned and I will tell you how. They would finish and then they'd put a plus there, a plus sign by the name of the person who was supposed to go, and if a person could not go then there would be a minus next to that person's name and then they would only convey to the messenger the following: No way should people by whose name there is a minus allow to go. So that is the way it was and then everybody did what they were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you would take over these lists, Mr. Vasovic, what would you do then with the lists?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: One list would stay with them. I would take another one back to the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who would you hand it over to?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Red Cross, the president of the Red Cross. I have nothing to do with that. I would just do whatever I was supposed to do and I would bring this back to the president of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, I'm just going to ask you in addition to these two localities where prisoners were held, did you visit the secondary school and the elementary school in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did. I was at the secondary school most often and also I went to the elementary school my very own school where I had taught but I spent most of my time at the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, on whose instructions did you go to those premises?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: According to the instructions of the president of the Red Cross it is not on anybody else's instructions that I went anywhere except the president of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Vasovic, what was the objective of your visits there?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the objective was first of all to talk to people about exchanges and everything but my major objective was to visit because I had many friends there, a great many friends. Secondly, they called me the International Red Cross there and now why, if you like, I can explain that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We are not going to go into all those details now, but I'm strictly interested in all your assignments within the Red Cross. Did you bring food to these people, can you tell me something about that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Food by all means, first of all food from the Red Cross but they got two meals at first from the central kitchen and then one and in order to supplement this because they were doing quite poorly from the point of view of health and any other point of view, we brought food to them from the Red Cross; however, what was most important was the following: Everybody knew this, but nobody opposed this as a matter of fact, people were pleased that it was so. From Zasavica, I mean that's where parents were, brothers or sisters of many of the people who were there, now when I would come with the delivery vehicle they were asking me, Sveto please could you take this to my brother or my husband or whoever, I mean it doesn't really matter. And then I would load up that delivery vehicle almost every day and then I'd bring all these things to the secondary school. The police were there, but there were some policemen who were so rigorous that there were all kinds of dialogue taking place there but nevertheless, they would let me go in or actually, I would get all these bags out with the food, meat, et cetera, and then this would be distributed to everybody individually, to all the persons to whom this was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is this the time to adjourn now or rather take the break or are we going to take the break later in view of the fact that we started late?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, we will stick to our schedule. We will take the break now and continue at 1615 hours. --- Break taken at 3.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasovic, before the break, we were talking about your visits to these places where civilians were kept. I think you gave us detailed answers and explained everything about this topic. Did you hear why these people were imprisoned, why were they held? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what I heard, it was that they were in possession of weapons and that they probably belonged to certain units, this is based on the stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is both for people who were in the elementary and the high school?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, when was the first time that you actively began to take part in the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Actively at the end of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the question, I mean the end of the answer, can he repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, could you please, so that we don't make problems for the interpreters, could you please wait a couple of seconds after my question, we are speaking the same language and we understand one another, could you please just make a pause of two seconds after the question before you start your answer and could you now please repeat what was the month that you said?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I started to work in the commission at the end of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what year was this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, you said that you know Miroslav Tadic. Did Miroslav Tadic also work on these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Miroslav Tadic did, was he negotiating, did he go with you to visit these detention units or did he do something else?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he ever went to any of the places where the people were detained, but he talked and negotiated with the other side regarding the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who else negotiated with him, with the other side?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Veljo Maslic, Velimir Maslic negotiated with the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when Veljo Maslic began to be more active on these activities regarding the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he started doing that a little bit later than I did, but he talked with Brko regarding all of these things that had to do with the exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you say Brko, who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, can you please tell me, at one point in the autumn of 1992, did Velimir Maslic receive an appointment?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: I think that in the beginning of October, he took over as president of the exchange commission. I think that that's when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, earlier in your testimony, when you talked about the civilians who applied to go on the exchange lists, you said that those people came and applied and said that they wanted to leave Samac and I'm thinking of civilians?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At the same time, you said that they were also sought from the other side?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also convey that to those people, did you tell them that they were being sought and who was seeking them?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were always informed that they were being sought and who was seeking them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the same case with the detainees, did you also tell them that they -- that the other side was looking for them?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document D96/3 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, do you know any of the people on this list?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is this what the list looked like when people applied; is that one of those lists?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes all the lists were almost the same as this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it states here who is looking for the person as well as the particulars of the person?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We won't be needing this document anymore. I've finished with this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, when the whole procedure is finished that you talked about when the lists are completed and agreed with on the -- with the other side, what is then the procedure that follows after that? Who informs these people that they can cross over to the other side, who informs the civilians and who informs the detainees?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: The civilians were most often informed by the local community messenger and I would inform all the people that I knew. I would take it upon myself to inform them, the time of departure and all of that, and the others were informed by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the detainees?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, when you went to the places where the detainees were and when you informed them that the other side was interested in having them cross over, were there any people who said that they did not wish to go over to the other side?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, of course. And there were people who had expressed this wish before, that they didn't want to go to the exchange still we had to tell them that they had to go there and say so and then they could come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, when people were informed that the place of exchange was set and when they were informed that they were to be exchanged - now we're talking about civilians - what was the procedure at the departure point, who called the people out to enter the buses?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Usually we would gather in front of the elementary or the high school. The buses would come there and all the people who were on the exchange list were there. I was the one who called out the civilians. I would call out each civilian, there was a policeman at the door who would check what things were being taken out and then the person would enter. That's the procedure as far as the civilians are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the policeman checked the things that were being taken out, what did you mean? What did he look at?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: He would look at the things that the person was taking out, the personal -- the hand luggage [as interpreted], that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, did you ever check the hand luggage of the people who were entering the buses?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never did. I wasn't interested in doing that. Why would I look at other people's things?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And did Miroslav Tadic ever do that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was never there. He was never there. How could he have looked when he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a correction on the translation, page 13, line 23, the witness said -- the witness said luggage and it was interpreted as hand luggage. So it should be luggage and it should be specified what this luggage looked like so that we can clarify anything in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, what did these people carry with them when they entered the bus?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly they carried their clothes and food, mostly clothes and food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did they have suitcases, bags, travel bags?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They had suitcases and big travelling bags.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, these people who were detained, how did they enter the buses, who brought them?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: We were separated, the police was over there and they were carrying out their work. They had nothing to do with the civilian part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Other than the fact that they went in the same buses?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same buses. They would all go together, both buses or three buses, however many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, when you were working, did it ever happen to you that a person who was on the list was taken off by the police before entering the bus?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never had anything like that happen to me while I was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that a person who was not on the list who you did not call out would enter the bus?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No, this was not possible because I didn't have the right to allow them to enter the bus, nor would I allow them to enter the bus because I would be the one who would be responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, did you or anybody else amongst you, during the actual application for the exchange or while entering the bus, did you ever tell any of those people that they did not have to go to the exchange?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the number of the buses, whether it was one or two, so I was the person in charge of the trip as a representative of the Red Cross so I would enter the bus and I would explain to them, "You are all going for an exchange. Those who wish to return can say so on the spot where the exchange is being carried out that they want to return. And in that case they will be allowed to return." So I would in the same way go on to the other bus and say the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell that to the detainees as well?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: To everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell the detainees that if they said that they did not want to be exchanged that they would be returned to detention or did you tell them something else?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: No. All of those who were returning would be returning directly to their homes. They would not go back to detention. I can give you an example, Ivica Kikic came back to his house and the next day, he came and he hugged me and he kissed me and he said, "Well, I went back to my house. I returned to my house."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So these people, the detainees knew before they arrived at the place of exchange that if they said that they did not want to cross over to the other side, that they would be freed?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Krgovic. I wonder, Mr. Vasovic, if you remember, this Mr. Kikic you mention, where had he been detained?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: In the high school. I think that's where he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And do you recall how he looked?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Very bad. He's a lovely man by heart, but he wasn't pleasant to look at, let me put it that way, he was very seriously ill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And what age would he have been; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Between 45 and 50. That's -- I think that's about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And just one last question, if you recall, you say he was very seriously ill, was this a medical condition he had or was he ill for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: It was an illness that he had. It was not -- he wasn't ill right at that moment, it was an illness that he had had from before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just one last question: Do you recall whether he mentioned to you whether he had been beaten while he was in detention in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't ever say anything like that to me, even though we were very good friends, extremely good friends, the two of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, and what happened then? Where did you go for the exchanges, which locations?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Where we left and where we were going to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What was the final destination?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR VASOVIC
utterances.text: Dragalic and Lipovac on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
